quests.hint: The study of ideas and existence. It has two ph's, and both say /f/.
quests.explanation: Phil-os-o-phy comes from Greek philos (loving) and sophia (wisdom). The first ph is at the start, and the second is in the ending -phy.

quests.hint: The study of land and places. It has two g's: one soft and one hard.
quests.explanation: Ge-og-ra-phy: geo (earth) + graphy (writing). The first g says /dʒ/, the second says /g/, and the ph says /f/.

quests.hint: Numbers and equations. It has four syllables, though many people say three.
quests.explanation: Math-e-mat-ics has an e in the second syllable that is often skipped in speech. It has to be written, or you end up with 'mathmatics'.

quests.hint: To go forward. It ends in -ceed, not -cede.
quests.explanation: Only three English words end in -ceed: proceed, exceed and succeed. Almost all other similar words end in -cede.

quests.hint: To go beyond a limit. It ends in the same -ceed as 'proceed'.
quests.explanation: Ex + ceed: this is one of the three -ceed words. The prefix ex- means 'out'.

quests.hint: To come before something. Unlike 'proceed', it ends in -cede.
quests.explanation: Pre + cede uses the normal -cede ending, as in recede and concede. The prefix pre- means 'before', so the word shares its idea with 'preview'.

quests.hint: To oversee work. In every variety of English, it ends in -ise.
quests.explanation: Super (over) + vise (see): supervise. Words with the -vise ending are always spelled -ise, such as revise and advise.

quests.hint: An agreement in which each side gives something up. It ends in -ise everywhere.
quests.explanation: Com-pro-mise ends in -mise. Like promise and premise, it is never spelled -ize.

quests.hint: To create on the spot, without preparing. It ends in -ise, as in 'supervise'.
quests.explanation: Im-pro-vise comes from Latin improvisus (unforeseen). The -vise ending is always -ise, so the spelling has no variants.

quests.hint: A group of similar things. It ends in -ory, not -ary.
quests.explanation: Cat-e-go-ry ends in -ory, said /əri/, as in history and factory. It is a weak ending that speech does not reveal.

quests.hint: A place where the dead are buried. It has three e's in the first three syllables, and no a.
quests.explanation: Cem-e-ter-y has e in each of the first three syllables and ends in -ery. 'Cemetary' is the classic error.

quests.hint: Required by rule. It ends in -ory, and it comes from a Latin verb meaning 'to order'.
quests.explanation: Man-da-to-ry ends in -ory, as in compulsory and satisfactory. The a in the second syllable is from mandare.

quests.hint: Worth wanting. The verb 'desire' loses its e before the suffix.
quests.explanation: Desire + able drops the e: desirable. The e is dropped before a vowel suffix, so 'desireable' is an error.

quests.hint: Impossible to say no to. It has a double r and an -ible ending.
quests.explanation: Ir + resist + ible: the rr comes from the prefix meeting the base, and the ending is -ible, although resist is a real word.

quests.hint: Absolutely necessary. The ending is -able, not -ible.
quests.explanation: In + dis + pens + able: the ending is -able. The spelling 'indispensible' is very common, but it is nonstandard.

quests.hint: The ability to learn and understand. The adjective behind it ends in -ent.
quests.explanation: Intelligent becomes intelligence: -ent turns into -ence. The word has a double l in the middle: in-tel-li-gence.

quests.hint: Willingness to accept differences. Its verb ends in -ate, but the noun does not take -ation.
quests.explanation: Tolerate loses -ate and takes -ance: tolerance. Most -ate verbs take -ation instead (educate, education), so this one needs to be learned separately.

quests.hint: Advice or direction. The verb 'guide' loses its e.
quests.explanation: Guide + ance drops the e: guidance. The u after g keeps the g hard, as in guide.

quests.hint: Not connected to the matter. It has a double r at the start and ends in -ant.
quests.explanation: Ir + relevant: rr comes from the prefix meeting the base. Relevant ends in -ant, so 'irrelevent' is an error.

quests.hint: A new idea or method. It has a double n in the middle.
quests.explanation: In + nov + ation: nn comes from the prefix in- meeting nov-, from the Latin for 'new'. The ending is -ation.

quests.hint: To light up. The prefix in- takes a different form here.
quests.explanation: Il + lumin + ate: the prefix in- becomes il- before l, giving ll. The root lumin means 'light'.

quests.hint: The top surface of a room. After c, the long e is spelled ei.
quests.explanation: Ceiling has ei after c, as in receive. The ending -ing is added to ceil.

quests.hint: A group of related living things. Here the ie follows c, which breaks a rhyme.
quests.explanation: Spe-cies has ie after c, an exception to the 'i before e, except after c' rule. The singular and plural have the same spelling.

quests.hint: A nutrient in meat and beans. The vowel /iː/ is spelled ei, with no c before it.
quests.explanation: Pro-tein has ei for /iː/, as in seize and either. There is no rule that predicts it.

quests.hint: A loan for buying a home. It has a t that is not pronounced.
quests.explanation: Mort-gage: the t is silent in /ˈmɔːɡɪdʒ/, and the ending -gage says /ɡɪdʒ/. The word comes from Old French 'dead pledge'.

quests.hint: A cabinet for dishes. It sounds like 'cubbard', but a p is written in the middle.
quests.explanation: Cup + board: it is a compound whose pronunciation has worn down to /ˈkʌbəd/. The spelling still holds both source words.

quests.hint: A vertical pillar, or a section of print. Ends with a letter you do not hear.
quests.explanation: Col-umn has a silent n after m, as in autumn. The n is heard in related forms such as columnist.

quests.hint: Impossible to confuse or miss. It comes from the verb 'mistake'; look at what happens to its e.
quests.explanation: Un + mistake + able: the e drops, giving unmistakable. The un- adds no letter change.

quests.hint: Easy to reach or use. It has a double c, a double s and an -ible ending.
quests.explanation: Ac-ces-si-ble has cc and ss, and it ends in -ible. Spell-checkers often flag 'accessable'.

quests.hint: An observable event or fact. It has ph, and its plural is 'phenomena'.
quests.explanation: Phe-nom-e-non has ph for /f/ and ends in -non. It is a Greek word, and the plural keeps the Greek ending -na.
